_comment: DESIGN.md §11.5. Sends cost gems, add monsters to a target opponent's next wave, and grant the sender permanent passive income in gold. The defender always gets the kill bounty. ONE MONSTER PER SEND: a tap used to buy a whole pack, which made the cheapest send the one that put six bodies in somebody's lane for eighteen gems and made every send a decision about a pack rather than about a monster. One tap, one body - so pressure is something a player builds up rather than drops, and the button has room to say what the thing it sends actually does. Costs and income were divided by the old pack sizes, so the gems and gold per monster are exactly what they were. Placeholders, like every number in data/.
_tuning: §11.5 asks for a payback period of roughly 5-6 waves, so that an early send is an economic investment and a late one is a pure attack. Income is sized against unit prices rather than against the gem cost, because the two currencies are not interchangeable: grub_pack at 10 gold a wave buys a 40g hammer in four waves, and is noise against late-game prices. That is the intended arc - clearly correct before wave 10, clearly a weapon after wave 14.
_vision: §12: some send types grant temporary sight of the target's lane. The cheap probe and the expensive raid do; the bread-and-butter sends do not, so vision is a thing you pay for rather than a side effect of attacking.
_abilities: §11.5, extended. Three of the five sends hand an ability to every monster they deliver (abilities.json), which is what makes a send a THING rather than a quantity of monsters: the same husk that walks in with a wave arrives braced when it is paid for. Putting the difference on the send rather than on a duplicate monster definition means one entry to tune and no second husk to keep in step with the first. The probe and the grub pack carry nothing - they are economy, not attacks.
